OCI image extraction creates symlink with absolute path target (CWE-61 primitive) AIExploitation High
Detects the Boxlite OCI layer extractor creating symlinks during tar processing where the link target points outside the staging directory (absolute path under /etc, /root, /home, /var/spool/cron, etc.). This is the core CVE-2026-46703 primitive — the unvalidated symlink target in apply_oci_layer() that turns a subsequent regular-file tar entry into an arbitrary host file write. Rationale: Article names the vulnerable binary explicitly (boxlite) and the exploit primitive's effect (writes outside dest staging dir into host paths like /etc/passwd, /root/.ssh/authorized_keys). The detection pivots on these two facts together — a high-fidelity pair because legitimate Boxlite extraction only writes inside its staging directory (typically /tmp/<sandbox-id>/ or /var/lib/boxlite/), never into /etc or /root. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f396-4rp4-7v2j
ATT&CKT1611 T1574 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Boxlite administrator manually copying configuration files into /etc/boxlite/ during install/upgrade
  • Custom Boxlite deployments that legitimately stage images under non-default paths (rare; would warrant tuning)
  • Security researcher locally reproducing the PoC in a contained test VM
  • Boxlite write-access to /var/lib/boxlite/* mis-pathed in the filter (false positive of the filter, not the detection — refine startswith list)
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath startswith "/etc/boxlite/" or FolderPath startswith "/var/lib/boxlite/")
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--install", "--upgrade", "--config-init"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Pull the full SyslogMessage / AdditionalFields for the alert and identify the OCI image digest Boxlite was extracting at the time (search for `extract_layer_tarball_streaming` or registry pull logs from the same host within the prior 5 minutes). Inspect the target path to determine impact (authorized_keys = RCE, /etc/passwd = account takeover, /etc/sudoers.d = privesc). Step 2 (Contain): Stop the boxlite service on the affected host (`systemctl stop boxlite`), quarantine the malicious image hash from the host's image cache, and roll back the modified host file from backup. If /root/.ssh/authorized_keys was touched, rotate SSH keys and audit access. Step 3 (Hunt): Pivot on the OCI image digest across all hosts running Boxlite to find other infected nodes; query registry/proxy logs for the image's pull URL to identify upstream distribution; check for any process executed as root within 60s of the write that may indicate successful RCE.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "boxlite"
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated", "SymbolicLinkCreated")
| where FolderPath startswith "/etc/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/root/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/home/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/var/spool/cron/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/etc/cron.d/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/etc/sudoers.d/"
   or FolderPath startswith "/etc/systemd/system/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "boxlite"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("symlink", "symlinkat", "linkat")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/", "/root/", "/home/", "/var/spool/cron", "/etc/cron.d", "/etc/sudoers.d", "/etc/systemd/system")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Boxlite sandbox writes to SSH authorized_keys (post-exploit RCE pivot) AIInstallation High
Detects the Boxlite service writing to any authorized_keys file on the host — the article explicitly calls out this technique as the RCE pivot ('writing the attacker's public key into the host's authorized_keys'). Since Boxlite has no legitimate reason to touch user SSH key files outside its sandboxed Box filesystems, any such write is high-confidence post-exploitation of CVE-2026-46703. Rationale: Article body explicitly cites this technique: 'The attacker can further leverage this capability to achieve remote code execution, such as writing the attacker's public key into the host's authorized_keys.' Boxlite is a container sandbox — it has zero legitimate workflow that involves writing to /root/.ssh/ or /home/*/.ssh/ on the host, making this a clean alerting signal. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f396-4rp4-7v2j
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Boxlite developer running PoC test in isolated lab environment
  • Sysadmin manually mis-using boxlite binary to copy files (extremely unlikely workflow)
  • Boxlite future feature adds legitimate SSH key sharing into Boxes (would require explicit re-tuning)
  • Symlink farms in user home dirs where authorized_keys is a link to a path Boxlite legitimately stages (none observed in default deployments)
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Capture the modified authorized_keys file immediately (`cp /root/.ssh/authorized_keys /tmp/ir-$(date +%s).authkeys`) and diff against the last known-good backup to identify the attacker's pubkey. Note the timestamp and correlate with Boxlite OCI image pulls in the prior 10 minutes — extract the image manifest digest. Step 2 (Contain): Remove the attacker-added pubkey from authorized_keys, kill any active SSH sessions from unknown IPs (`who`, `last`, `ss -tnp`), rotate the user's SSH keys, and block the malicious OCI image hash at the registry / image-pull policy layer. Step 3 (Hunt): Search across the fleet for the same OCI image digest and the same attacker pubkey in authorized_keys files; query egress logs for outbound SSH connections from any host with Boxlite installed in the last 30 days; review Boxlite version inventory and patch to fix for CVE-2026-46703.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "boxlite"
| where FileName =~ "authorized_keys" or FolderPath has "/.ssh/authorized_keys"
| where ActionType in~ ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "SymbolicLinkCreated")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AdditionalFields
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "boxlite"
| where SyslogMessage has "authorized_keys"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54") or SHA1 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54") or MD5 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54") or SHA1 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54") or MD5 in~ ("b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b673b4e3400c71bd72464c98610c952e2164f70f946873b82adf3e6212851d54"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Twig package (CVE-2026-46633) installed (twig/twig < 3.26.0) AIExploitation High
Surface assets where Microsoft Defender TVM reports the Twig PHP templating library at a version vulnerable to CVE-2026-46633. Exploitation gives RCE via single-quote injection in a `{% use %}` template name; SecurityPolicy allows `{% use %}` even under sandbox, so any application that accepts attacker-influenced template names against twig/twig < 3.26.0 is reachable. Prioritise patching to 3.26.0 or later. Rationale: Article is a vendor advisory: identifies the exact package (composer:twig/twig), fixed version (3.26.0), and CVE (CVE-2026-46633). The only high-fidelity, non-generic detection from this content is asset coverage — every other behaviour-based UC (PHP web server spawning shells, web-shell cache file writes) collapses into generic web-shell rules already shipped, which the prompt explicitly excludes. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7p85-w9px-jpjp
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM picks up `twig/twig` development copies in non-production scratch directories (developer laptops) where the dependency is pinned but not exposed externally
  • Lab / sandbox VMs that intentionally host vulnerable packages for security research
  • Vendored or vendored-and-forked copies of Twig embedded inside larger PHP applications (e.g., Symfony, Drupal, Shopware) where the parent product's own patched release supersedes the bundled version but TVM still reports the bundled string
  • Stale TVM scan data on decommissioned hosts that have already been re-imaged but not yet aged out of the inventory table

// Exclude developer / non-production hosts via MachineGroup tagging
| where DeviceName !has "dev-" and DeviceName !has "-lab"
// Exclude assets tagged as decommissioned in your CMDB join

1. Triage: confirm the asset is internet-facing or accepts external user input that flows into a Twig template loader (look for application owner in CMDB; check WAF / reverse-proxy logs for the host). Validate the reported `SoftwareVersion` is below 3.26.0 and not a vendored copy already patched by a parent product release. 2. Contain: if internet-facing and unpatched, request an emergency patch ticket to upgrade twig/twig to >= 3.26.0; in the interim, validate that no application surface passes user-controlled strings into `{% use %}` template names and add a WAF rule blocking request bodies containing `{% use '` with a single-quote inside a template name argument. 3. Hunt: pivot to DeviceProcessEvents for the affected host(s) and look for the PHP-FPM / Apache / Nginx process tree spawning `sh`, `bash`, `cmd.exe`, or `powershell.exe` in the past 30 days — any such tree post-dating the vulnerable version's first install is a possible exploitation event worth deeper forensic review.

AWS IAM role trust policy created with set-qualified operator on GitHub OIDC sub claim AIInstallation High
Hunts the exact misconfiguration class that @hulumi/policies <1.3.2 failed to flag: CreateRole/UpdateAssumeRolePolicy CloudTrail events whose trust policy uses ForAnyValue:StringLike / ForAllValues:StringLike / ForAllValues:StringEquals against token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub. Any role created with this shape — particularly with wildcards in the sub value — is assumable by GitHub Actions workflows the role owner never intended to authorize. Rationale: Article specifies the exact unsafe pattern: set-qualified operators (ForAnyValue:StringLike etc.) applied to token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub bypass the inspector. CloudTrail's CreateRole/UpdateAssumeRolePolicy carries the full policyDocument as JSON — substring matching for both the operator family AND the OIDC sub claim string is high-fidelity because the combination is essentially never seen in correctly-authored trust policies (canonical pattern is the bare StringLike or StringEquals). Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/avoiding-mistakes-with-aws-oidc-integration-conditions • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/configuring-openid-connect-in-amazon-web-services
ATT&CKT1098.003 T1199 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate use of ForAnyValue:StringLike to match the sub claim against a constrained array of specific repo+branch values (e.g. matching exactly two protected branches) — not an actual bypass but matches the query
  • Internal Terraform/CDK modules that templatize trust policies and emit ForAnyValue:StringLike even when only a single sub value is being matched
  • Cross-account/role-consolidation pipelines that intentionally use ForAnyValue:StringLike across a curated allowlist of GitHub repos belonging to the same engineering org
  • DR/test-account replays of role creation as part of disaster-recovery validation (same policy shape, expected event)
Suppression filter
| where NOT match(policyDocument, "(?i)token\.actions\.githubusercontent\.com:sub\"\s*:\s*\[\s*\"repo:[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+/[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+:(ref:refs/heads/[a-zA-Z0-9._/-]+|environment:[a-zA-Z0-9._-]+|pull_request)\"")
Response runbook
Triage: pull the full policyDocument from the CloudTrail event; extract the sub claim values inside the set-qualified operator. If any value contains an unanchored wildcard (`*`, `repo:*`, `repo:org/*:*`) or is missing entirely, treat as confirmed unsafe. Contain: revert the trust policy via UpdateAssumeRolePolicy to the prior known-good version (use CloudTrail's prior policyDocument value), or detach the role temporarily by attaching a Deny-all permissions boundary while you investigate the assumer identity. Hunt: enumerate all sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity calls against this role's ARN for the last 90 days; cross-reference the assumed sub claims against your expected GitHub org/repo allowlist; pivot on any unexpected actor to find downstream AWS API calls made under the assumed credentials.
title: AWS IAM Role Trust Policy Uses Set-Qualified Operator on GitHub OIDC Sub Claim
id: 8e0e8b9b-7d5f-4f6a-9d2e-3f2c5a1b7e44
description: Detects CreateRole / UpdateAssumeRolePolicy CloudTrail events whose policy document uses set-qualified string operators (ForAnyValue / ForAllValues) on token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub — the misconfiguration class that @hulumi/policies <1.3.2 (GHSA-q2f7-m237-v562) failed to flag.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q2f7-m237-v562
  - https://www.wiz.io/blog/avoiding-mistakes-with-aws-oidc-integration-conditions
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/22
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1098.003
  - attack.t1199
  - attack.t1078.004
logsource:
  product: aws
  service: cloudtrail
detection:
  selection_event:
    eventSource: 'iam.amazonaws.com'
    eventName:
      - 'CreateRole'
      - 'UpdateAssumeRolePolicy'
  selection_operator:
    requestParameters.policyDocument|contains:
      - 'ForAnyValue:StringLike'
      - 'ForAnyValue:StringEquals'
      - 'ForAllValues:StringLike'
      - 'ForAllValues:StringEquals'
  selection_oidc:
    requestParameters.policyDocument|contains: 'token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub'
  condition: all of selection_*
level: high
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:(CreateRole OR UpdateAssumeRolePolicy) @requestParameters.policyDocument:(*ForAnyValue\:StringLike* OR *ForAnyValue\:StringEquals* OR *ForAllValues\:StringLike* OR *ForAllValues\:StringEquals*) @requestParameters.policyDocument:*token.actions.githubusercontent.com\:sub*
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Changes.command) as policyDocument values(All_Changes.user) as user values(All_Changes.src) as src_ip values(All_Changes.user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.object_category="role" All_Changes.action IN ("created","modified","updated") All_Changes.vendor_product="AWS CloudTrail" by All_Changes.object
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)`
| where match(policyDocument, "(?i)(ForAnyValue|ForAllValues):String(Like|Equals)") AND match(policyDocument, "(?i)token\.actions\.githubusercontent\.com:sub")
| eval has_wildcard_sub=if(match(policyDocument, "(?i)token\.actions\.githubusercontent\.com:sub[^,}]*\*"),"yes","no")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| table firstTime, lastTime, object, user, src_ip, user_agent, has_wildcard_sub, policyDocument
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Changes.command) as policyDocument values(All_Changes.user) as user values(All_Changes.src) as src_ip values(All_Changes.user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.object_category="role" All_Changes.action IN ("created","modified","updated") All_Changes.vendor_product="AWS CloudTrail" by All_Changes.object
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)`
| where match(policyDocument, "(?i)(ForAnyValue|ForAllValues):String(Like|Equals)") AND match(policyDocument, "(?i)token\.actions\.githubusercontent\.com:sub")
| eval has_wildcard_sub=if(match(policyDocument, "(?i)token\.actions\.githubusercontent\.com:sub[^,}]*\*"),"yes","no")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| table firstTime, lastTime, object, user, src_ip, user_agent, has_wildcard_sub, policyDocument
AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity from GitHub OIDC with unexpected repo/branch sub claim AIExploitation Medium
Downstream hunt for actor abuse of a role whose unsafe trust policy slipped past @hulumi/policies <1.3.2. Pivots on sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity events where the WebIdentity issuer is token.actions.githubusercontent.com and the asserted sub claim does not match the org's approved GitHub repo allowlist — flagging the first-time-seen repo+role pairs that an attacker exploiting a wildcard sub policy would generate. Rationale: The article's bypass directly enables GitHub Actions OIDC sub-claim impersonation against IAM roles. AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity is the actor-observable consequence — the userIdentity.userName field on the CloudTrail event carries the asserted sub (e.g. repo:owner/repo:ref:refs/heads/main). Anti-joining against an approved-org/repo lookup is the cleanest baseline-deviation pivot for catching exploitation of an unsafe policy that the scanner missed. Cross-referenced with the AWS GitHub OIDC docs and the Wiz misconfiguration write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/avoiding-mistakes-with-aws-oidc-integration-conditions • https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/configuring-openid-connect-in-amazon-web-services
ATT&CKT1199 T1078.004 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • New legitimate repository onboarding that hasn't been added to the approved_github_oidc_roles lookup yet
  • Fork-based PR workflows where the sub claim format is 'repo:org/repo:pull_request' rather than the usual ref:refs/heads/* pattern
  • Renamed/migrated GitHub repositories where the sub claim now references the new org/name and the lookup is stale
  • Self-hosted GitHub Enterprise instances using a different OIDC issuer URL whose sub claim format diverges from cloud GitHub
  • Reusable workflows invoked from a different upstream repo (sub claim points at the caller, which may be unlisted)
Response runbook
Triage: extract the gh_org/gh_repo/gh_ref tuple from the userIdentity.userName claim and compare to the org's approved repo registry; check the trust policy of the assumed role for the unsafe set-qualified operator pattern from UC1; review the source IP and user-agent (legitimate GitHub Actions runners emit a recognizable UA). Contain: if the assumer is unauthorized, immediately revoke active sessions via `aws iam put-role-policy` attaching a Deny-all inline policy, then rotate the role's trust policy to a strict StringEquals sub claim; if confirmed-malicious, also revoke any short-lived credentials the actor minted via subsequent sts: calls. Hunt: enumerate all AWS API calls performed under the assumed-role session ID for the past 30 days; look for data egress (s3:GetObject, s3:CopyObject), credential creation (iam:CreateAccessKey, sts:GetSessionToken), and persistence (iam:AttachRolePolicy, lambda:CreateFunction with the assumed role); audit every other IAM role with a similar trust-
source:cloudtrail @evt.name:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity @userIdentity.type:WebIdentityUser @requestParameters.roleArn:* @requestParameters.webIdentityToken:* -@userIdentity.userName:(repo\:approved-org/* OR repo\:another-approved-org/*) @evt.outcome:success
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Authentication.src) as src_ip values(Authentication.user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.signature="AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity" Authentication.vendor_product="AWS CloudTrail" by Authentication.dest, Authentication.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| rex field=user "repo:(?<gh_org>[^/]+)/(?<gh_repo>[^:]+):(?<gh_ref>.+)"
| where isnotnull(gh_org)
| lookup approved_github_oidc_roles role_arn AS dest OUTPUT allowed_orgs, allowed_repos
| where isnull(allowed_orgs) OR NOT match(gh_org, allowed_orgs) OR (isnotnull(allowed_repos) AND NOT match(gh_repo, allowed_repos))
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| table firstTime, lastTime, dest, gh_org, gh_repo, gh_ref, src_ip, user_agent, count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Authentication.src) as src_ip values(Authentication.user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action="success" Authentication.signature="AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity" Authentication.vendor_product="AWS CloudTrail" by Authentication.dest, Authentication.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| rex field=user "repo:(?<gh_org>[^/]+)/(?<gh_repo>[^:]+):(?<gh_ref>.+)"
| where isnotnull(gh_org)
| lookup approved_github_oidc_roles role_arn AS dest OUTPUT allowed_orgs, allowed_repos
| where isnull(allowed_orgs) OR NOT match(gh_org, allowed_orgs) OR (isnotnull(allowed_repos) AND NOT match(gh_repo, allowed_repos))
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| table firstTime, lastTime, dest, gh_org, gh_repo, gh_ref, src_ip, user_agent, count

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

CVE-2026-46614: Unauthorized /fission-function/ invocation on Fission router public listener (port 8888) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to the internal-style /fission-function/<ns>/<name> route on the Fission router's public listener (svc/router, port 8888). On versions <= 1.22.0 this route is mounted on the public listener and allows any caller reaching the router to invoke any Function object — bypassing HTTPTrigger host/path/method restrictions. Post-fix (v1.23.0+), this path should only exist on port 8889 (svc/router-internal, ClusterIP-only), so any hit on port 8888 is either an unpatched cluster being exploited or an enumeration probe. Rationale: The path string `/fission-function/` and port 8888 are both directly named in the GHSA advisory as the vulnerable surface (pkg/router/httpTriggers.go:280-284 and svc/router listener config). After v1.23.0 this path should only appear on port 8889 (svc/router-internal), so hits on 8888 are unambiguous - either an exploitation attempt or an unpatched cluster still serving the route. We exclude 404 because that's enumeration covered by the next UC; 200 means successful unauthorized invocation, 502 means the function exists and went cold (still a successful enumeration). Defender KQL is empty because Fission runs on Linux K8s nodes and the relevant telemetry is HTTP-layer (ingress/WAF), not endpoint EDR. Falcon LogScale is empty for the same reason - FDR doesn't ship ingress HTTP path data. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/fission/fission/releases/tag/v1.23.0 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3g33-6vg6-27m8
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal trigger sources (kubewatcher, timer, mqtrigger, mqt-keda pods) misrouted to the public 8888 listener instead of the new svc/router-internal:8889 after a partial upgrade
  • Authorized security scans / pentests probing the Fission attack surface
  • Operators running curl health-check scripts against /fission-function/<ns>/<name> from inside the cluster for testing
  • Legacy CI/CD pipelines that pre-date HTTPTrigger objects and still invoke functions via the internal path
  • Cluster federation / multi-cluster controllers that proxy /fission-function/ requests across namespaces
Suppression filter
// Suppress known internal trigger pods if their source IPs are stable and documented
| where SourceIP !in ("<kubewatcher-pod-ip>", "<timer-pod-ip>", "<mqtrigger-pod-ip>", "<mqt-keda-pod-ip>")
// Suppress authorized scanner User-Agents
| where RequestClientApplication !has "Nessus" and RequestClientApplication !has "Qualys" and RequestClientApplication !has "kube-probe"
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Confirm the Fission release version on the destination cluster (`kubectl -n fission get deploy router -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'`). If <= 1.22.0 the route is unauthenticated by design - any non-cluster source IP is suspicious. Resolve SourceIP - internal trigger pods (kubewatcher/timer/mqtrigger) are expected; everything else is not. 2. CONTAIN: Apply the GHSA-3g33-6vg6-27m8 mitigation immediately - add a NetworkPolicy blocking ingress to svc/router:8888 except from the project's ingress controller, and add an ingress path-filter dropping /fission-function/* externally. Schedule upgrade to v1.23.0+ within the change window. 3. HUNT: Pivot on SourceIP - list every other distinct URL it hit, every distinct namespace it accessed via /fission-function/<ns>/, and any 2xx responses (= successful invocation). Pull function-pod logs for the targeted functions to see what code ran and what data egressed.
// Fission runs on Kubernetes (Linux) - this detection lives in ingress/WAF logs forwarded to CommonSecurityLog or web-tier IIS logs in front of the router
union isfuzzy=true
(
  CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where RequestURL has "/fission-function/"
  | where DestinationPort == 8888 or isempty(tostring(DestinationPort))
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, EventOutcome, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, RequestClientApplication
  | extend Verdict = case(EventOutcome has "200", "Successful unauthorized invocation", EventOutcome has "502", "Cold-start - function exists", EventOutcome has "404", "Probe miss", "Other - verify")
),
(
  W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where csUriStem has "/fission-function/"
  | where sPort == 8888
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP=cIP, DestinationIP=Computer, DestinationPort=sPort, RequestMethod=csMethod, RequestURL=strcat(csUriStem, iff(isnotempty(csUriQuery), strcat("?",csUriQuery), "")), EventOutcome=tostring(scStatus), DeviceVendor="Microsoft", DeviceProduct="IIS", RequestClientApplication=csUserAgent
  | extend Verdict = case(EventOutcome == "200", "Successful unauthorized invocation", EventOutcome == "502", "Cold-start - function exists", EventOutcome == "404", "Probe miss", "Other - verify")
)
| where Verdict != "Probe miss"   // 200/502 = signal; 404 alone is enumeration noise covered by UC2
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Fission Router Unauthorized Function Invocation via /fission-function/ Path (CVE-2026-46614)
id: a7c4e9d2-3b8f-4c2a-91e7-fb7d6a8c1e3f
description: Detects HTTP requests to the /fission-function/<ns>/<name> path on the Fission router public listener (port 8888). On vulnerable versions (<= 1.22.0) this allows direct invocation of any Function without HTTPTrigger restrictions. Post-fix the path moved to internal port 8889 - so any hit on 8888 indicates exploitation or an unpatched cluster.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3g33-6vg6-27m8
  - https://github.com/fission/fission/releases/tag/v1.23.0
author: Detection Engineering

  selection_port:

  condition: selection_path and selection_port and not filter_probe_miss
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate internal trigger sources (kubewatcher / timer / mqtrigger) misconfigured to hit the public listener instead of the new svc/router-internal:8889
  - Penetration tests / vulnerability scans authorized against the cluster
level: high
(source:nginx OR source:kubernetes) @http.url_details.path:*/fission-function/* @network.destination.port:8888 -@http.status_code:404

Fission Function Name Enumeration via /fission-function/ Probing (CVE-2026-46614 recon) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects function-name discovery against the Fission router by counting distinct /fission-function/<ns>/<name> paths probed from the same source within a short window. Per the advisory, callers can enumerate which functions exist by differentiating response semantics (404 = no such function, 200 = invoked, 502 = function exists and went cold). A burst of 404s interleaved with 200/502s from one source is the canonical recon shape. Rationale: The advisory explicitly calls out enumeration as an impact: 'Enumerate function names by probing the response semantics (404 vs 200 vs 502 from cold start).' Counting distinct paths under /fission-function/ per source IP in a short window directly models that pattern; requiring at least 3 404s alongside the path-count threshold filters legitimate trigger callers (who hit known paths and don't miss). Sigma is empty because this is a count/threshold detection, not single-event-shape. Defender and Falcon are empty because the telemetry sits at the ingress/WAF layer, not on endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/fission/fission/releases/tag/v1.23.0 • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3g33-6vg6-27m8
ATT&CKT1595.003 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Trivy, kube-bench) walking /fission-function/<ns>/<name> with a wordlist as part of an authorized assessment
  • CI/CD smoke tests that iterate through known function names to validate post-deploy health (legitimate, but indistinguishable from enumeration by path-count alone)
  • Multi-tenant cluster operators using a single audit-bot identity to walk all namespaces' functions for inventory
  • Misconfigured load-test tools (k6, locust) generating high distinct-path counts against a function under test
  • Service mesh / sidecar retries on 502 inflating the apparent unique-path count when retries rewrite URL segments
Suppression filter
// Suppress scanner User-Agents if your scanners are documented
| where UserAgent !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Trivy", "kube-bench", "OpenVAS")
// Suppress documented CI/CD smoke-test source IPs
| where SourceIP !in ("<ci-runner-ip-range>")
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Inspect the SourceIP - is it on the org's scanner allowlist? Pull the User-Agent and pivot on whether it asserts itself as a scanner (Nessus/Qualys/curl/python-requests). Check whether the hit responses include 200s - successful invocations after enumeration are the genuine concern. 2. CONTAIN: Rate-limit /fission-function/* at the ingress immediately (e.g. nginx limit_req_zone keyed by source IP), then apply the CVE-2026-46614 fix - either upgrade Fission to >= 1.23.0 or apply the path-block NetworkPolicy from the advisory mitigation section. 3. HUNT: For every function name the enumeration successfully invoked (200/502), pull the function's pod logs to determine what code ran; check whether the function references secrets, mounts credentials, or makes outbound calls. Pivot on SourceIP across the past 30 days to see prior reconnaissance.
let LookbackHours = 24h;
let WindowMinutes = 10m;
let MinUniquePaths = 5;
let MinProbeMisses = 3;
union isfuzzy=true
(
  CommonSecurityLog

  | where RequestURL has "/fission-function/"
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, RequestURL, Status=tostring(EventOutcome), UserAgent=RequestClientApplication, Router=DestinationIP
),
(
  W3CIISLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackHours)
  | where csUriStem has "/fission-function/"
  | where sPort == 8888
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP=cIP, RequestURL=csUriStem, Status=tostring(scStatus), UserAgent=csUserAgent, Router=Computer
)
| summarize
    UniqueFunctionPaths = dcount(RequestURL),
    TotalRequests = count(),
    HitFunctions = dcountif(RequestURL, Status in ("200","502")),
    MissFunctions = dcountif(RequestURL, Status == "404"),
    SamplePaths = make_set(RequestURL, 20),
    UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5),
    Routers = make_set(Router, 3)

| where UniqueFunctionPaths >= MinUniquePaths and MissFunctions >= MinProbeMisses

    HitFunctions > 0 and MissFunctions >= 3, "High - mixed 200/502 hits with 404 misses (likely successful enumeration)",
    MissFunctions >= 10, "Medium - heavy 404 probing",
    "Low")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

BadIIS rogue native module drop in IIS folders (demo.pdb / Chinese path heuristic) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts non-trusted writes of DLL/native modules into IIS-served directories (\inetsrv\, \inetpub\wwwroot\bin\), and image loads by w3wp.exe of modules outside the canonical IIS install paths or whose file path contains Han/CJK characters. Targets the Talos-described BadIIS commodity variant whose modules carry 'demo.pdb' strings and Chinese-language folder paths. Rationale: Article explicitly names 'demo.pdb' strings and Chinese-language folder paths inside IIS binaries as the Talos-recommended hunt hooks. Standard EDR can't search PDB strings inline, so we proxy with (a) writes of native modules into IIS paths by non-installer processes and (b) the CJK Unicode range (\u4e00-\u9fff) in module paths, which catches the Chinese-folder-path signal directly. Memory mem-1304 already corroborated BadIIS as commodity MaaS infrastructure.
ATT&CKT1505.004 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web-app CI/CD pipelines (Octopus, Azure DevOps, TeamCity) that xcopy assemblies into \inetpub\wwwroot\bin\
  • Custom in-house IIS native module installers that don't use msiexec or appcmd
  • Internationalised IIS deployments where customer site assets legitimately contain Chinese folder names (CN/HK/TW tenants)
  • WebDeploy (msdeploy.exe) pushes outside the trusted-installer allowlist
  • Manual sysadmin DLL replacement during ARR / URL Rewrite module troubleshooting
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msdeploy.exe","octopus.tentacle.exe","agent.listener.exe","buildagent.exe")) and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("appcmd install module","msdeploy.exe -verb:sync"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the dropped DLL hash and run it through VT/Talos Reputation; check whether it loads in w3wp.exe via DeviceImageLoadEvents; inspect file strings for 'demo.pdb' or other PDB paths to confirm. Step 2 — Contain: if unsigned and loaded by w3wp, isolate the IIS host, snapshot its inetsrv\config\applicationHost.config to capture rogue native-module registration, and pull the DLL for analysis. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on writer process + writer SHA256 across all internet-facing IIS hosts; review outbound network from w3wp.exe for redirect destinations (SEO-fraud targets); audit applicationHost.config and globalModules sections fleet-wide for unauthorized entries.
let IISWriters = dynamic(["msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","drvinst.exe","appcmd.exe","windowsupdatebox.exe","tiworker.exe"]);

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="FileWrite";
let ModuleLoads = DeviceImageLoadEvents

   or (not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Windows\System32\inetsrv\") and not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\") and not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Program Files\") and not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Program Files (x86)\") and not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Windows\WinSxS\") and not(FolderPath startswith_cs @"C:\Windows\assembly\"))

Talos weekly prevalent-malware hash hit (Coinminer worm / TunMirror / SECOH-QAD / KMS-Loader) AIInstallation High
Hash IOC sweep for the five Talos-published prevalent-malware SHA256s for the week ending May 21 2026: Win.Worm.Coinminer (VID001.exe), PUA.Win.Tool.Tunmirror (TunMirror.exe), Win.Tool.Procpatcher (SECOH-QAD.exe), and the KM-prefixed sample. Covers process execution, file writes, and DLL/EXE module loads to surface infection regardless of stage. Rationale: Direct hash IOCs published by Cisco Talos with detection name + sample filename per hash. These are the week's top prevalent samples — VID001.exe (Coinminer worm), TunMirror.exe (network tunneling PUA), SECOH-QAD.exe (KMS-emulation tooling), KM-prefix loader. Hash equality is the highest-fidelity detection shape possible. Cross-checked against: • https://talosintelligence.com/talos_file_reputation?s=9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1496 T1027.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandboxed malware analysis VMs where analysts intentionally execute these binaries
  • AV signature-feed VMs that detonate samples for engine validation
  • Internal red-team kit that ships SECOH-QAD or similar KMS-emulators for licensing-bypass testing (rare and policy-prohibited)
  • Talos-feed test endpoints that pre-deploy IOCs to validate detection coverage
Suppression filter
and not (DeviceName has_any ("-sandbox","-malwarelab","detlab-","-vt-")) and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("vmtoolsd.exe","cuckoo-agent.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm hash match against the Talos advisory; pull the file path, executing user, and parent process from the hit; check whether the host is a known sandbox/lab. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the endpoint, quarantine the file via Defender Live Response or CrowdStrike RTR (`falconctl quarantine`), suspend any logon session running the binary, and reset the affected user's password (TunMirror/Coinminer often arrive bundled with credential-stealers). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the binary's parent process and the writing process across all hosts for the past 30 days; check for follow-on outbound connections to mining pools (stratum+tcp/3333/4444/5555/14444/14433) or proxy domains; review scheduled tasks and Run keys created within ±1h of the hash hit.

BadIIS traffic-hijacking: IIS 503 surge + anomalous external redirect ratio per site/hour AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Talos-described BadIIS impact pattern: hijacked IIS servers throwing 503 spikes (proxy/upstream failure) while also emitting an unusually high ratio of 30x/redirect responses pointing visitors to attacker-controlled SEO-fraud destinations. Aggregates per site per hour and flags hours that materially deviate from the per-site baseline. Rationale: Article explicitly tells defenders to 'actively monitor IIS environments for unauthorized traffic redirection, unexpected reverse proxying, or sudden spikes in 503 Service Unavailable errors' — this query is a direct expression of that guidance, anchored on per-site/per-hour anomalies versus a 30-day baseline so it doesn't fire on legitimately redirect-heavy sites. Datadog and Falcon LogScale fields left empty because raw IIS W3C access logs are not part of the standard FDR feed and are not in the Datadog source list provided.
ATT&CKT1496 T1565.002 T1090
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate marketing-site URL-shortener / vanity-redirect bins (e.g. /go/* paths returning 302)
  • App-pool restart / app deployment causing genuine 503 surge on a single host
  • Upstream database outage causing IIS to return 503 across the app pool (correlate with DB telemetry)
  • Geo-redirect logic returning 302 to localised subdomains for new-country traffic launches
  • Health-check endpoints that intentionally return 503 during maintenance windows
Suppression filter
| where not(sSiteName has_any ("healthcheck","shortener","go.","link.")) | where not(SampleReferers has_any ("google.","bing.","yandex."))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the top destination Locations / Refresh headers from the 3xx responses in the affected hour and check whether they point to known-good in-org domains or external SEO/gambling/affiliate domains; correlate with UC1 to see if the same host had a recent BadIIS-style module drop. Step 2 — Contain: if redirect destinations are external and unsanctioned, take the IIS app pool offline, snapshot applicationHost.config + globalModules + the bin/ contents, and rotate any service-account credentials the worker process had. Step 3 — Hunt: extract the rogue native-module DLL hash and pivot fleet-wide via UC1 + UC2; review the IIS host's outbound DNS for the past 7 days for suspicious lookups (especially Chinese-language SEO-spam TLDs); audit IIS extensibility (ISAPI filters, HTTP modules, URL Rewrite outbound rules) for entries added outside change-management windows.
let lookback = 7d;
let bucket = 1h;
let BadIISSignals = W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csMethod in~ ("GET","HEAD","POST")
| summarize Total = count(),
           Status503 = countif(scStatus == 503),
           Status3xx = countif(scStatus between (300 .. 399)),
           DistinctClients = dcount(cIP),
           DistinctURIs = dcount(csUriStem),
           SampleUserAgents = make_set(csUserAgent, 5),
           SampleReferers = make_set(csReferer, 5)
           by Computer, sSiteName, bin(TimeGenerated, bucket)
| extend PctErr503 = round((Status503 * 100.0) / Total, 2),
         PctRedirect = round((Status3xx * 100.0) / Total, 2)
| where (Status503 >= 50 and PctErr503 >= 20) or (Status3xx >= 100 and PctRedirect >= 40);
let Baseline = W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(lookback))
| summarize BaselineTotal = count(),
           BaselineRedirect = countif(scStatus between (300 .. 399)),
           Baseline503 = countif(scStatus == 503)
           by Computer, sSiteName
| extend BaselinePctRedirect = round((BaselineRedirect * 100.0) / BaselineTotal, 2),
         BaselinePctErr503 = round((Baseline503 * 100.0) / BaselineTotal, 2);
BadIISSignals
| join kind=leftouter Baseline on Computer, sSiteName
| where PctRedirect >= (coalesce(BaselinePctRedirect, 0.0) * 3) or PctErr503 >= (coalesce(BaselinePctErr503, 0.0) * 3)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, Total, Status503, Status3xx, PctErr503, PctRedirect, BaselinePctRedirect, BaselinePctErr503, DistinctClients, DistinctURIs, SampleUserAgents, SampleReferers
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count as Total, count(eval('Web.status'==503)) as Status503, count(eval(in('Web.status',301,302,303,307,308))) as RedirectCount, dc(Web.dest) as DistinctOriginHosts, values(Web.uri_path) as SampleURIs, values(Web.dest) as Destinations from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method="GET" by Web.src Web.site _time span=1h | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | eval PctErr503 = round((Status503*100.0)/Total, 2), PctRedirect = round((RedirectCount*100.0)/Total, 2) | where (Status503 >= 50 AND PctErr503 >= 20) OR (RedirectCount >= 100 AND PctRedirect >= 40) | sort - _time

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["9f1f11a708d393e0a4109ae189bc64f1f3e312653dcf317a2bd406f18ffcc507", "d87e8d9d43758ce67a8052cb2334b99cc24f9b0437ee44815f360be0b22d835a", "9896a6fcb9bb5ac1ec5297b4a65be3f647589adf7c37b45f3f7466decd6a4a7f", "acd55c44b8b0d66d66defed85ca18082c092f048d3621da827fce593305c11fd", "96fa6a7714670823c83099ea01d24d6d3ae8fef027f01a4ddac14f123b1c9974", "2915b3f8b703eb744fc54c81f4a9c67f", "362498c3e71eeaa066a67e4a3f981d1c", "38de5b216c33833af710e88f7f64fc98", "0f03f72a92aef6d63eb74e73f8ac201d", "aac3165ece2959f39ff98334618d10d9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

5 Supply Chain Attacks in 48 Hours: Why Securing One Layer Is Not Enough

StepSecurity
2026-05-21 10 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A poisoned VS Code extension breached GitHub. A trojanized PyPI package hit Microsoft. Compromised GitHub Actions and a self-spreading npm worm targeted thousands more. In just 48 hours, attackers hit every layer of the software development pipeline. Traditional security tools did not stop any of it.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised Nx Console VS Code extension (nrwl.angular-console v18.94.0/18.95.0/18.100.0) install on endpoint
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Known Shai-Hulud / Nx Console implant hash match (SHA256/SHA1) · [LLM] macOS LaunchAgent/LaunchDaemon plist persistence pointing at Python interpreter · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Nx Console / Shai-Hulud C2 connection (t.m-kosche.com, check.git-service.com, filev2.getsession.org, api.masscan.cloud, 83.142.209.194) · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Developer credential store read by Python or Node spawned from VS Code (Nx Console stealer pattern) · [LLM] GitHub audit log bulk private-repo clone burst (post Nx Console compromise pattern)
Compromised Nx Console VS Code extension (nrwl.angular-console v18.94.0/18.95.0/18.100.0) install on endpoint AIDelivery High
Detects writes/installations of the malicious Nx Console extension versions published to the VS Code Marketplace on May 18, 2026. Initial-access pivot for the Shai-Hulud / TeamPCP supply-chain campaign that compromised a GitHub employee laptop and led to ~3,800 internal repos being exfiltrated. Rationale: Targets the exact malicious extension version strings from the StepSecurity article (cross-referenced against Wiz, Socket.dev, and JFrog vendor write-ups in session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1287); developer endpoints almost never receive a freshly published Nx Console version within hours of release so the temporal-uniqueness of these specific versions makes this very low FP. We also covered the two neighbour versions (18.94.0 / 18.100.0) StepSecurity flagged as also impacted. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/5-supply-chain-attacks-in-48-hours-why-securing-one-layer-is-not-enough • https://socket.dev/blog/nx-console-malicious-package
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher pulling the malicious extension into a sandbox VM for reverse engineering
  • Threat intel team mirroring the marketplace artifact for IOC enrichment
  • Internal red team replaying the attack chain in a purple-team exercise
  • An internal cache/proxy snapshot of the marketplace replaying the old version metadata on backup restore
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountUpn in~ ("redteam@contoso.com","malware-lab@contoso.com")) and not (DeviceName startswith "SANDBOX-" or DeviceName startswith "REVENG-")
Response runbook
1. Triage: Pull DeviceFileEvents and DeviceProcessEvents for the device for ±2h around the install; confirm the file SHA matches one of the known stealer hashes (see UC2) and that VS Code's Code Helper is the writing process. Pull DeviceInfo to identify whether the user is a developer / engineering org member. 2. Contain: Isolate the device via Defender Live Response (or MDM); revoke all GitHub PATs, SSH keys, AWS access keys, npm tokens for the user; force AAD/Okta password+MFA reset; remove the extension via `code --uninstall-extension nrwl.angular-console`. 3. Hunt: Sweep the org for any other device that ever installed nrwl.angular-console between 2026-05-18 and 2026-05-20; pivot to UC3 (C2 IOCs) and UC6 (bulk GitHub clones from this user) to scope post-exploitation activity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
    or FileName has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Code","Code Helper","code","code-helper","Code.exe")
    or FolderPath has_any (".vscode/extensions","\\.vscode\\extensions\\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, SHA1
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
    or TargetFileName has_any ("nrwl.angular-console-18.95.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.94.0","nrwl.angular-console-18.100.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256, TargetFileSHA1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known Shai-Hulud / Nx Console implant hash match (SHA256/SHA1) AIInstallation Medium
Hash-based catch-all for the 8 SHA256 and 7 SHA1 implant artifacts attributed to the May 2026 Nx Console / TeamPCP supply-chain attack. Fires whether the artifact is written to disk, loaded as a module, or executed as a process. Rationale: Hashes drawn directly from the StepSecurity pre-extracted IOC bundle for the article (corroborated against Wiz, Datadog, and JFrog vendor analyses in session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1285). Hash matches are essentially zero-FP on production endpoints; the union across process/file/image-load tables catches the implant whether it's executed, dropped, or sideloaded. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/5-supply-chain-attacks-in-48-hours-why-securing-one-layer-is-not-enough • https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/nx-console-shai-hulud-analysis
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Reverse-engineering sandbox VM detonating the sample
  • CrowdStrike/Defender threat-hunt team replaying the artifact for IOC tuning
  • Backup-restore replay of a quarantined Defender sample triggering a re-scan
  • Malware-museum / IR-training lab images carrying the hash in a vault
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName startswith "SANDBOX-" or DeviceName startswith "REVENG-" or DeviceName startswith "MWLAB-") and not (InitiatingProcessAccountUpn in~ ("redteam@contoso.com","malware-lab@contoso.com"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Confirm host is a real production endpoint (not a sandbox via DeviceInfo.DeviceCategory / device naming); correlate with UC1 to determine if the malicious extension was the entry vector; pull the parent process chain to map the kill chain. 2. Contain: Isolate via Defender network-isolation; rotate every credential the user touched in last 30d (GitHub PATs, SSH keys, ~/.aws, ~/.npmrc, Okta/AAD password, AAD refresh tokens via revokeSignInSessions); for macOS hosts also revoke iCloud Keychain access. 3. Hunt: Pivot to UC3 (C2 IOCs), UC4 (LaunchAgent persistence) and UC6 (GitHub bulk clones) using the same UPN/AccountUpn; sweep the device images directory for any other extension installed within 48h of the malicious one — TeamPCP have shown ability to bundle multiple compromised IDE extensions.

  (DeviceProcessEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where SHA256 in (StealerSHA256) or SHA1 in (StealerSHA1) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in (StealerSHA256) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in (StealerSHA1)
   | extend Source="DeviceProcessEvents"

   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)

   | extend Source="DeviceImageLoadEvents"
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, SHA1, Source)

Nx Console / Shai-Hulud C2 connection (t.m-kosche.com, check.git-service.com, filev2.getsession.org, api.masscan.cloud, 83.142.209.194) AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound network or DNS activity to any of the 4 known C2 domains or the dedicated IP used by the May 2026 Nx Console credential stealer. Covers HTTPS exfil, GitHub-API-shaped C2 (api.masscan.cloud), and the resolver side of DNS tunneling. Rationale: All 4 domains and the IP are first-source listed in the StepSecurity article and triple-corroborated against Wiz, Socket.dev, and Datadog write-ups (session memory observations 1281, 1284, 1287). t.m-kosche.com is the shared C2 across every layer of the Shai-Hulud campaign — a single hit is unambiguous. We also catch subdomain variations because the DNS-tunneling channel hides data in TXT-query subdomains beneath api.masscan.cloud. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/nx-console-supply-chain-attack • https://socket.dev/blog/nx-console-malicious-package • https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/nx-console-shai-hulud-analysis
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst manually browsing the IOC to confirm site is offline
  • Sinkhole/passive-DNS infrastructure resolving the domain
  • Network sandbox detonation of the sample replaying C2 callouts
  • Internal honeypot relay that intentionally resolves known-bad domains for tracking
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","safari") and InitiatingProcessAccountUpn in~ ("threatintel@contoso.com","soc-analyst@contoso.com"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: Identify the initiating process — if it's `Code Helper`, `node`, or `python` on a developer endpoint, treat as critical and pivot directly to UC1 (extension install) and UC2 (hash match). Pull DeviceNetworkEvents for the device for ±24h to spot longer C2 cadence. 2. Contain: Sinkhole all 4 domains at corporate DNS; null-route 83.142.209.194 at the edge; isolate the originating endpoint via Defender; revoke all credentials accessible from the device. 3. Hunt: Sweep DNS logs across the whole org for the last 30d for any other host that resolved these domains, even once; pivot to GitHub audit logs (UC6) for the affected user looking for repo-clone bursts during the C2 window.
let C2Domains = dynamic(["t.m-kosche.com","check.git-service.com","filev2.getsession.org","api.masscan.cloud"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["83.142.209.194"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and (RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains))) or (RemoteIP in (C2IPs))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domains = dynamic(["t.m-kosche.com","check.git-service.com","filev2.getsession.org","api.masscan.cloud"]);
let C2IPs = dynamic(["83.142.209.194"]);
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DnsQuery has_any (C2Domains)
   | extend Source="DNS", IndicatorMatched=DnsQuery
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, IndicatorMatched, Source),
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DstHostname has_any (C2Domains) or DstIpAddr in (C2IPs) or Url has_any (C2Domains)
   | extend Source="Network", IndicatorMatched=coalesce(DstHostname, DstIpAddr)
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, IndicatorMatched, Source),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationHostName has_any (C2Domains) or DestinationIP in (C2IPs) or RequestURL has_any (C2Domains)
   | extend Source="Proxy/Firewall", IndicatorMatched=coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestURL)
   | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, IndicatorMatched, Source)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
